title: Temiya's silence
hook: a baby prince sees what a throne requires, and decides never to speak.
tomorrow: what is a whole day like with plain food and no entertainment?

segments.voice: Yesterday, nekkhamma: let it go, a loss until you've seen what it trades for. Today, the great renunciation story of this block, and its strangest hero.

Everyone has sat through a group chat where the smartest move was not to reply. So why would a prince pretend for years that he couldn't speak? In the Temiya Jataka, he's a baby on his father's lap when he watches the king hand down harsh punishments to thieves. A gentle word for parents: that's as dark as the story gets. The baby remembers, the story says, a past life when he sat on that same throne, and what came after it. So he decides: he will never be king.
screen: `THE MOVE IS NOT TO REPLY.` → `A BABY ON THE KING'S LAP.` → `HE WILL NEVER BE KING.`

segments.voice: So Temiya goes silent, and limp, as if he can neither hear nor speak nor walk. The court tests him for years, with treats, with frights, with temptations. He never breaks. At last the king is told to have him buried, and the charioteer Sunanda drives him to the forest and starts digging. Then Temiya stands, lifts the chariot, and speaks. He tells Sunanda he isn't dull or mute; he stayed silent to escape a throne. He becomes a forest ascetic, and in the end his parents follow him there. He renounced the throne. Now the wisdom in it. Temiya's silence isn't a rule that silence is always better; when the time comes, he speaks. In another sutta, the Buddha says he speaks only what is true and helpful, and knows the right time to say it. A neighbor tradition says something close. Ecclesiastes, in the Hebrew Bible that Jews and Christians both read, sets out the seasons of a life, and among them: "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." Both texts treat silence as a choice with a right time, not an empty space. The honest difference: Ecclesiastes sets those times inside a world God has ordered, a season to everything under heaven. Temiya's silence is one long refusal, so he won't be pulled into cruelty and the suffering that follows it.
screen: `SILENT, LIMP, UNBROKEN.` · `AT THE GRAVE, HE SPEAKS.` · `THE RIGHT TIME TO SPEAK.` · `ECCLESIASTES: A TIME TO KEEP SILENCE.` · then, large: `HE RENOUNCED THE THRONE.`

segments.voice: For this sit, keep a silence on purpose: not just quiet, but chosen. Notice the words that rise and want out, and let each one pass unspoken. When the bell ends, choose your first words carefully, and let them be true and kind.
Temiya's silence: a prince who stayed silent for years to escape a throne, then spoke at the grave. Renunciation, kept to the very end.
Keep close: he renounced the throne, and chose his moment to speak. Day eight of thirty.

screen: `DAY 1553 COUNTS.` → `THE TEN PERFECTIONS · DAY 8 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: A WHOLE DAY OF PLAIN FOOD AND NO ENTERTAINMENT?`

howItsDone: The Temiya Jataka is told and painted in Theravada temples as the perfection of renunciation; some Buddhists keep periods of noble silence on retreats, speaking only when needed.

chat.meaning: Ecclesiastes and Temiya's story both honor a right time for silence. They differ in why: God's seasons, or refusing cruelty.
